nameStory: Canadian burnet gets its name from its northern range, extending from Canada down through New England. The "burnet" part comes from the Old French "brunette," meaning "little brown one," referring to the brownish color the flower spikes turn as they age and dry.
description: Canadian burnet is a tall, graceful wildflower that can surprise you with its height - reaching 4 to 5 feet tall in ideal conditions. It's a member of the rose family, though you might not guess it at first glance. The plant produces distinctive creamy white flower spikes that look like fuzzy bottle brushes or cotton swabs, blooming from summer into fall. Despite being in the rose family, it has compound leaves that look more like those of a small tree than a typical wildflower.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Creamy white, cylindrical spikes that look like fluffy bottle brushes, 2-6 inches long. The tiny individual flowers are densely packed and feel soft to the touch, with prominent white stamens giving the spike its fuzzy appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and stately, growing 4-5 feet high with an upright, branching stem. The plant has a distinctive architectural look, standing well above most other wetland wildflowers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into 7-17 oval leaflets with toothed edges. The leaflets feel smooth and have a subtle cucumber-like scent when crushed, though they taste quite bitter.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, reddish-green stems that are sturdy and hollow. The stems often have a slight zigzag pattern between leaf nodes and feel firm when gently squeezed.

habitat: Canadian burnet thrives in wet places - look for it in bogs, swamps, wet meadows, and along roadside ditches where water collects. It prefers full sun to partial shade and acidic, mucky soils that stay consistently moist. You'll often find it growing alongside other wetland plants like cattails, sedges, and joe-pye weed.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as compound leaves unfurl from the base. Young plants are much shorter and easily overlooked among other emerging wetland vegetation.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive white bottle-brush flower spikes begin appearing in mid to late summer, making this the best time for identification. Plants reach their full impressive height.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into early fall, gradually turning brown as seeds develop. The tall dried stems with their brown seed heads become prominent landscape features.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads often persist above snow, creating distinctive silhouettes in winter wetlands. The brown, cylindrical seed heads are still recognizable.

funFact: Despite being in the rose family alongside apples, roses, and strawberries, Canadian burnet's flowers have no petals at all - those fluffy white "petals" you see are actually just the stamens (male flower parts) sticking out, creating nature's own bottle brush!
confusionNotes: The tall white flower spikes might remind you of other wetland plants, but Canadian burnet's bottle-brush flowers are unique in New England wetlands. The closest look-alike might be meadowsweet, but meadowsweet has frothy, cloud-like flower clusters rather than the neat cylindrical spikes of burnet.
contextualKnowledge: Unlike its European relatives salad burnet and great burnet, Canadian burnet requires cooking to remove bitterness before eating - never try the raw leaves as a trail snack. The name "burnet" has confused some people into thinking it's related to other "burn" plants, but it's purely coincidental.
compareHints: Canadian burnet is the tallest burnet species you'll find in New England, easily distinguished from its relatives by its creamy white flowers (great burnet has dark red flowers, while salad burnet has tiny greenish flowers with red tips). It's also the only burnet that commonly grows in wet habitats - the others prefer drier soils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Great burnet towers over its relatives, reaching 3-6 feet compared to Canadian burnet's 2-4 feet and salad burnet's modest 1-2 feet.
Unlike its relatives Canadian burnet and great burnet which are native and have white or pink flowers, salad burnet has those distinctive dark crimson flower heads and is much smaller overall.
Siberian Burnet is the only burnet in New England with drooping flower spikes - all other burnets have upright flower heads.
